models.collectorNote: Brass-era aristocracy with a finite, documented survivor pool. Provenance and correctness define value; the London-to-Brighton Run keeps them exercised and visible.

generations.name: Model R 'Curved Dash'
generations.note: About 19,000 were built across the run — unprecedented volume. A horizontal single-cylinder engine under the seat, tiller steering, and the curved dash that named it.

models.intro: The car that started mass production's story: a $650 single-cylinder runabout built in the thousands while rivals built dozens — the first Oldsmobile, and for a while the best-selling car in America.
models.name: Curved Dash Oldsmobile

models.collectorNote: Early Rocket 88s are the historically important buy — the later cars are cruise-night staples. Originality of the Rocket engine is the check.

generations.name: Rocket 88 (first generation)
generations.note: The 303 Rocket V8 made 135 hp when flathead Fords made 100, in a car a class lighter than the big Oldsmobiles it shared the engine with. NASCAR noticed immediately; so did every young engineer in Detroit.

models.intro: The 1949 Rocket 88 — a modern overhead-valve V8 in the lighter body — is a founding document of the muscle-car idea and the subject of what is often called the first rock-and-roll record. The 88 nameplate then ran for fifty years.
models.name: 88 / Rocket 88

models.collectorNote: W-30 convertibles are the summit; documentation is everything in a field full of tributes. The nameplate continued as a trim into the 1990s — the atlas covers the muscle-era cars.

generations.name: 4-4-2 (first era)
generations.note: The 400 V8 reached 350 hp in tri-carb 1966 form (L69). W-30 ram-air packages began the factory hot-rod escalation.

generations.name: 4-4-2 (second era)
generations.note: The 455 arrived for 1970, rated up to 370 hp in W-30 trim with its fibreglass hood and red inner fenders. The Hurst/Olds editions bookend the era in silver and gold.

models.intro: Four-barrel, four-speed, dual exhausts — the name was the spec sheet. Born as a police-package option in the GTO's shadow, the 4-4-2 became its own model and, in 455 W-30 form, one of the era's fastest.

models.collectorNote: First-generation cars are design icons with a following to match. The chain-drive transaxle is durable; trim and vacuum-operated details are the restoration cost.

generations.name: Toronado (first generation)
generations.note: 425 cu in and 375 hp through the front wheels, with handling that shamed its size. The 1968 and 1970 facelifts kept the silhouette; the W-34 option sharpened the original further.

models.intro: The car that brought front-wheel drive back to America: a 7-litre V8 driving the front wheels through a chain-driven transaxle, styled like a jet-age sculpture. It worked, it sold, and it changed GM's engineering map.
models.name: Toronado

generations.name: Cutlass (G-body era)
generations.note: The downsized rear-drive Cutlass Supreme was America's best-selling car in several of these years. The Hurst/Olds and 4-4-2 revivals kept the performance thread; diesels are the footnote.

models.intro: For a time, the Cutlass was simply the best-selling car in America — the nameplate that carried Oldsmobile's volume from the muscle era through the G-body years, with the Supreme as the default upgrade buy of the suburbs.
models.name: Cutlass

models.collectorNote: First-generation Autobahn cars are the pick of a thin, appreciating field. Head-gasket and electronics diligence applies; the reward is a genuinely distinctive flagship.

generations.name: Aurora
generations.note: The 4.0 'Shortstar'-family V8 made 250 hp; the second generation (2001) added a V6 option and softened the design. Aurora pace cars led the Indy 500 — the engineering was real.

models.intro: Oldsmobile's last flagship and its best car in decades: a Northstar-derived 4.0 V8, a rigid shell, and concept-car styling — the car that was meant to save the marque and instead became its elegant farewell.
models.name: Aurora
